We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text. Consider a customer support system receiving the following message: "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers. llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0 > We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." , which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON. [Start thinking] ... [end thinking] ```json { "team_to_handle" : "Billing" , "urgency" : "High" , "request_refund" : true } But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } This is the key idea behind decision models . What are decision models? A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands. TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2). The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models ) For a decision model, the fundamental interface is: State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities Why not use LLMs for everything? We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks. However, there are a few problems with this approach. LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices. Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work. Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work. How are decision models different from classification models? Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification. Traditional classification Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments: Billing Technical support Sales A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution. The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head . If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model. Zero-shot classification Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time. For example: from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'], # 'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]} Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs. from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" , "legal" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'], # 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]} One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis. This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is. Where decision models differ Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul). More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions . Consider these three approaches: Property Classification Zero-shot classification Decision model Probability over choices Yes Yes Yes Labels defined at inference No Yes Yes Multiple typed questions No No Yes Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions Task-specific Possible with adaptation Native primitives The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions. The decision model interface A decision model request has the following two components: state questions State The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models. For example: { "customer_message" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "subscription" : "pro" , "previous_tickets" : 2 } Questions and their primitives Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions: Choice: Select one of several possible answers. Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale. Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically. Let's go over them one by one. Choice: A probability distribution over options Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification. Suppose we ask: Which department should handle this customer request? The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z 1 , … , z K z_1,\ldots,z_K z 1 ​ , … , z K ​ , (with K K K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax: p i = exp ⁡ ( z i ) ∑ j = 1 K exp ⁡ ( z j ) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} p i ​ = ∑ j = 1 K ​ exp ( z j ​ ) exp ( z i ​ ) ​ Here, K K K is the number of choices. Consider this illustrative distribution: Choice Probability Billing 0.998 Technical support 0.001 Sales 0.001 The probabilities sum to one: ∑ i = 1 K p i = 1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i = 1 ∑ K ​ p i ​ = 1. The model chooses the option with the largest probability: y ^ = arg ⁡ max ⁡ i p i \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y ^ ​ = ar g i max ​ p i ​ In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives. Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale? Consider the question: How urgent is this customer request? We define three levels: 0: Low urgency 1: Medium urgency 2: High urgency from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] }, } } ) # { # 'urgency': { # 'type': 'score', # 'score': 1.7053890228271484, # 'legend': { # '0': 'low', # '1': 'medium', # '2': 'high' # }, # 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814, # 'probabilities': { # '0': 0.014908230863511562, # '1': 0.26479458808898926, # '2': 0.7202972173690796 # } # } # } The model again produces a probability distribution: Level Probability 0 — Low 0.01 1 — Medium 0.26 2 — High 0.72 Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index . For a random variable X X X representing the level, the expectation is: E [ X ] = ∑ i = 0 K − 1 i p i \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E [ X ] = i = 0 ∑ K − 1 ​ i p i ​ For our example: E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.01 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.01 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 The reported score is therefore 1.7 . This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7. Noul: A Bernoulli decision The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question. For example: Is the customer requesting a refund? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } } ) # { # 'refund': { # 'type': 'noul', # 'noul': 0.9947046637535095 # } # } Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli). Let Y Y Y represent a binary outcome: Y ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p ) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y ∼ Bernoulli ( p ) where P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . If the model returns: { "type" : "noul" , "noul" : 0.92 } it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No. The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it. Confidence: How certain is the model? So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score. The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that. For a Choice with K K K options, the confidence is: p max ⁡ − 1 K 1 − 1 K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1 − K 1 ​ p m a x ​ − K 1 ​ ​ where p max ⁡ p_{\max} p m a x ​ is the largest predicted probability. The intuition here is: A uniform distribution has confidence 0. p max ⁡ = 1 K p_{\max} = \frac{1}{K} p m a x ​ = K 1 ​ . This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely. A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. p max ⁡ = 1 p_{\max} = 1 p m a x ​ = 1 The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence. In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998: C = 3 ( 0.998 ) − 1 2 = 0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C = 2 3 ( 0.998 ) − 1 ​ = 0.997 Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558. Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations. Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation . A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once: inference engines like llama.cpp can serve any decision model through the same API the Hub can package and surface them consistently and training tools can target shared primitives instead of individual architectures The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces. 1. Serving with Transformers Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline , AutoModelForDecision , and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) print (decide) # DecisionPipeline: {'model': 'JevForDecision', 'dtype': 'bfloat16', 'device': 'cuda', 'input_modalities': 'text'} One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so: from transformers import AutoModelForDecision, DecisionConfig model_id = "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" config = DecisionConfig.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(model_id) Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint . Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model. 2. Serving with llama.cpp llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API. For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF The default server runs on port 9931. items.content: Back to Articles Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models Published November 11, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 35 +29 Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors! Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget. In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4 , my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how. This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study , which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example. Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below. Pooling at inference Mean vectors Ordinary model Pooling-aware model Gain (points) Unpooled 193.22 51.84 52.39 +0.55 pool_factor=2 96.86 50.10 51.74 +1.64 pool_factor=3 64.74 49.70 51.45 +1.76 pool_factor=4 48.68 49.03 51.23 +2.20 pool_factor=5 39.04 48.13 50.28 +2.15 pool_factor=6 32.62 47.07 49.85 +2.78 max_tokens=64 54.76 49.27 50.89 +1.63 max_tokens=32 29.58 48.25 50.12 +1.87 max_tokens=16 15.60 46.61 49.26 +2.65 max_tokens=8 7.99 43.12 46.61 +3.48 max_tokens=4 4.00 37.22 43.00 +5.78 distance_threshold (calibrated) 54.76 50.10 51.24 +1.14 distance_threshold (calibrated) 29.58 48.38 50.96 +2.58 distance_threshold (calibrated) 15.60 47.23 49.63 +2.41 For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps. At the trained pool_factor=4 , nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39. The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget. Combining Compression Techniques If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order: Embedding quantization to 4, 2, or 1 bit(s), for example via Fast-PLAID , to reduce storage per coordinate. Token pooling to reduce the number of document vectors, optionally with pooling-aware fine-tuning as shown in this blog. Matryoshka token embeddings to reduce the dimensionality of each token vector, optionally with fine-tuning to preserve retrieval quality at smaller widths. If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus. MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings. Try the complete training example , choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model. With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical! References Stefan Josef. Learn to Pool: Lightweight Fine-Tuning for Flexible Multi-Vector Compression . items.content: Back to Articles The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Published November 12, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 26 +20 Suvaditya Mukherjee suvadityamuk Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository . If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works . Let’s go! Introduction 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. What we want to improve A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. What will we use? LoRA LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have: A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain from here Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3 , because DINOv3 is a gated model If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start. How TRELLIS.2 works Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. Encoding the input image First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage. O-Voxel and Structured Latents O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer. Geometry Generation (Shape Flow) The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512. We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape. Material Generation + Mesh Creation In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures. Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file. Planning Which components to fine-tune We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities. Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training. If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Why use LoRA Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more. What you’ll run A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning. To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub: Give the containers access to your data. Set the parameters for your task. Run the preprocessing container. Run the fine-tuning container. Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training. Experiment overview We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment: Prepare the data. Convert GLB or OBJ meshes into the latent representations TRELLIS.2 uses for training, and render the input images. Train the adapters. Run one job for each DiT, with the prepared dataset and a LoRA configuration. Explain the code. Examine how the containers load the data, add adapters, and train the models. We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it. Walkthrough Running on Hugging Face Jobs Preprocessing The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline . See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository . export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 6h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep \ --meshes your-username/my-meshes \ --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --private --holdout 0.05 \ --views 16 --workers 8 For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments: flag meaning -d Detach: print the job ID and URL, then return. To follow the job, run hf jobs logs -f <id> --flavor a100-large The hardware. We use a100-large (80 GB). To see all options, run hf jobs hardware --timeout 6h The job stops after this time. Both commands resume. Preprocessing skips finished objects. Training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to --secrets HF_TOKEN Send your token (from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login) to the job as an encrypted environment variable. The token is not written into the image cr.hf.co/...:latest The image to run. All text after it is the command that runs in the container This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here . The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later. LoRA Fine-tuning The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run. We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 If you set --push-to , the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity . A compact script is also available in the same repository . If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have , feel free to use the following set of commands. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For the Shape Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Running locally with Docker Preprocessing The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different. # For preprocessing into latents docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep --meshes your-username/my-meshes --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 LoRA Fine-tuning # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands: export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso Inside the training pipeline Preprocessing into latents We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again. We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training. Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train ( ss or shape ), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning. cfg = json.load( open ( { "ss" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/ss_flow_lora_gso.json" , "shape" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json" , }[FLOW] ) ) key, latents = { "ss" : ( "ss_latent" , "ss_latents/ss_enc_conv3d_16l8_fp16_64" ), "shape" : ( "shape_latent" , "shape_latents/shape_enc_next_dc_f16c32_fp16_512" ), }[FLOW] roots = json.dumps( { "gso" : { key: f" {DATA} / {latents} " , "render_cond" : f" {DATA} /renders_cond" , "meta" : DATA, } } ) ds = getattr (datasets, cfg[ "dataset" ])(roots, **cfg[ "dataset_args" ]) holdout = set ( open ( f" {DATA} /holdout.txt" ).read().split()) ds.instances = [(root, sha) for root, sha in ds.instances if sha not in holdout] batches = cycle( DataLoader( ds, batch_size=BATCH, shuffle= True , drop_last= True , num_workers= 4 , collate_fn= getattr (ds, "collate_fn" , None ), ) ) Preparing LoRA adapters We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model() . This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface. We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point ( fp32 ) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 ( bf16 ) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. model = models.from_pretrained(cfg[ "ckpt" ]) for block in model.blocks: block.use_checkpoint = True inject_adapter_in_model( LoraConfig( r=cfg[ "rank" ], lora_alpha=cfg[ "alpha" ], target_modules=cfg[ "lora_targets" ] ), model, ) params = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): p.requires_grad_( "lora_" in name) if p.requires_grad: p.data = p.data. float () # fp32 master weights for LoRA params.append(p) model.cuda().train() Training It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3 , Flux 2 , and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching. We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen. The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands. We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. opt = torch.optim.AdamW( params, lr=cfg[ "lr" ], weight_decay=cfg[ "weight_decay" ], betas=( 0.9 , 0.95 ) ) dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor( cfg[ "image_cond_model" ], image_size=cfg[ "image_size" ] ).cuda() We then follow these steps within the training loop: Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config). Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting. Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise). Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions. Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t ). def flow_loss ( x0, cond ): s = cfg[ "t_schedule" ] t = ( torch.rand(x0.shape[ 0 ]) if s[ "name" ] == "uniform" else torch.sigmoid( torch.randn(x0.shape[ 0 ]) * s[ "args" ][ "std" ] + s[ "args" ][ "mean" ] ) ) t = t.cuda() noise = ( x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats)) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else torch.randn_like(x0) ) tv = t.view(- 1 , *[ 1 ] * ( len (x0.shape) - 1 )) x_t = ( 1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg[ "sigma_min" ] + ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * tv) * noise pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000 , cond), ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * noise - x0 return ( F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else F.mse_loss(pred, target) ) The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches. For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps. for step in range ( 1 , STEPS + 1 ): for _ in range (ACCUM): batch = next (batches) x0 = recursive_to_device(batch[ "x_0" ], "cuda" ) with torch.no_grad(): cond = dino(batch[ "cond" ]) cond[torch.rand( len (cond), device= "cuda" ) < cfg[ "p_uncond" ]] = 0 with torch.autocast( "cuda" , dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg[ "grad_clip" ]) opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Results We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours. The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry. Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects. The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans. We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set: Metric What it means Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better. F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better. Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better. In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects. For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space . Future directions Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate job
items.raw_text: Back to Articles The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Published November 12, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 26 +20 Suvaditya Mukherjee suvadityamuk Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository . If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works . Let’s go! Introduction 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. What we want to improve A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. What will we use? LoRA LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have: A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain from here Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3 , because DINOv3 is a gated model If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start. How TRELLIS.2 works Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. Encoding the input image First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage. O-Voxel and Structured Latents O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer. Geometry Generation (Shape Flow) The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512. We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape. Material Generation + Mesh Creation In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures. Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file. Planning Which components to fine-tune We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities. Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training. If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Why use LoRA Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more. What you’ll run A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning. To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub: Give the containers access to your data. Set the parameters for your task. Run the preprocessing container. Run the fine-tuning container. Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training. Experiment overview We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment: Prepare the data. Convert GLB or OBJ meshes into the latent representations TRELLIS.2 uses for training, and render the input images. Train the adapters. Run one job for each DiT, with the prepared dataset and a LoRA configuration. Explain the code. Examine how the containers load the data, add adapters, and train the models. We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it. Walkthrough Running on Hugging Face Jobs Preprocessing The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline . See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository . export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 6h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep \ --meshes your-username/my-meshes \ --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --private --holdout 0.05 \ --views 16 --workers 8 For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments: flag meaning -d Detach: print the job ID and URL, then return. To follow the job, run hf jobs logs -f <id> --flavor a100-large The hardware. We use a100-large (80 GB). To see all options, run hf jobs hardware --timeout 6h The job stops after this time. Both commands resume. Preprocessing skips finished objects. Training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to --secrets HF_TOKEN Send your token (from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login) to the job as an encrypted environment variable. The token is not written into the image cr.hf.co/...:latest The image to run. All text after it is the command that runs in the container This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here . The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later. LoRA Fine-tuning The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run. We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 If you set --push-to , the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity . A compact script is also available in the same repository . If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have , feel free to use the following set of commands. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For the Shape Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Running locally with Docker Preprocessing The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different. # For preprocessing into latents docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep --meshes your-username/my-meshes --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 LoRA Fine-tuning # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands: export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso Inside the training pipeline Preprocessing into latents We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again. We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training. Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train ( ss or shape ), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning. cfg = json.load( open ( { "ss" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/ss_flow_lora_gso.json" , "shape" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json" , }[FLOW] ) ) key, latents = { "ss" : ( "ss_latent" , "ss_latents/ss_enc_conv3d_16l8_fp16_64" ), "shape" : ( "shape_latent" , "shape_latents/shape_enc_next_dc_f16c32_fp16_512" ), }[FLOW] roots = json.dumps( { "gso" : { key: f" {DATA} / {latents} " , "render_cond" : f" {DATA} /renders_cond" , "meta" : DATA, } } ) ds = getattr (datasets, cfg[ "dataset" ])(roots, **cfg[ "dataset_args" ]) holdout = set ( open ( f" {DATA} /holdout.txt" ).read().split()) ds.instances = [(root, sha) for root, sha in ds.instances if sha not in holdout] batches = cycle( DataLoader( ds, batch_size=BATCH, shuffle= True , drop_last= True , num_workers= 4 , collate_fn= getattr (ds, "collate_fn" , None ), ) ) Preparing LoRA adapters We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model() . This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface. We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point ( fp32 ) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 ( bf16 ) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. model = models.from_pretrained(cfg[ "ckpt" ]) for block in model.blocks: block.use_checkpoint = True inject_adapter_in_model( LoraConfig( r=cfg[ "rank" ], lora_alpha=cfg[ "alpha" ], target_modules=cfg[ "lora_targets" ] ), model, ) params = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): p.requires_grad_( "lora_" in name) if p.requires_grad: p.data = p.data. float () # fp32 master weights for LoRA params.append(p) model.cuda().train() Training It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3 , Flux 2 , and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching. We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen. The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands. We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. opt = torch.optim.AdamW( params, lr=cfg[ "lr" ], weight_decay=cfg[ "weight_decay" ], betas=( 0.9 , 0.95 ) ) dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor( cfg[ "image_cond_model" ], image_size=cfg[ "image_size" ] ).cuda() We then follow these steps within the training loop: Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config). Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting. Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise). Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions. Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t ). def flow_loss ( x0, cond ): s = cfg[ "t_schedule" ] t = ( torch.rand(x0.shape[ 0 ]) if s[ "name" ] == "uniform" else torch.sigmoid( torch.randn(x0.shape[ 0 ]) * s[ "args" ][ "std" ] + s[ "args" ][ "mean" ] ) ) t = t.cuda() noise = ( x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats)) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else torch.randn_like(x0) ) tv = t.view(- 1 , *[ 1 ] * ( len (x0.shape) - 1 )) x_t = ( 1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg[ "sigma_min" ] + ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * tv) * noise pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000 , cond), ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * noise - x0 return ( F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else F.mse_loss(pred, target) ) The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches. For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps. for step in range ( 1 , STEPS + 1 ): for _ in range (ACCUM): batch = next (batches) x0 = recursive_to_device(batch[ "x_0" ], "cuda" ) with torch.no_grad(): cond = dino(batch[ "cond" ]) cond[torch.rand( len (cond), device= "cuda" ) < cfg[ "p_uncond" ]] = 0 with torch.autocast( "cuda" , dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg[ "grad_clip" ]) opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Results We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours. The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry. Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects. The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans. We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set: Metric What it means Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better. F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better. Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better. In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects. For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space . Future directions Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate job

items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.18563 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Nov 2026] Title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion Authors: Daniel Grimm , Kyra Jongman , Renato Cordeiro Ferreira , Giuseppe Cascavilla , Alfredo Cuzzocrea , Willem-Jan Van Den Heuvel View a PDF of the paper titled Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion, by Daniel Grimm and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS–RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of 0.7776 0.7776 on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of 0.637 0.637 for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to 0.8580 0.8580 and AUC to 0.852 0.852 . Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision 0.9013 0.9013 , AUC 0.904 0.904 ), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it. Index Terms: AIS, dark vessels, maritime domain awareness, pair hidden Markov model, RF geolocation, sensor fusion I Introduction Global trade has relied on maritime transport for centuries. Today, an estimated 90 % 90\% of all international goods, ranging from raw materials to everyday products such as fruit and clothing, are transported by sea [ 1 ] . Maritime transport is attractive because vessels can carry large volumes of cargo over long distances at relatively low cost. However, the growing reliance on this mode of transportation, combined with other maritime traffic, has led to increased congestion at sea [ 2 ] . This is particularly evident near ports and in narrow waterways, where dense traffic heightens the risk of accidents. In addition to congestion, the vast and largely unregulated nature of the oceans facilitates illicit activities such as smuggling, unreported fishing, and sanctions evasion. Although initially designed as a collision-avoidance tool, authorities rely heavily on the Automatic Identification System (AIS) [ 3 , 4 ] for continuous vessel tracking. AIS transponders broadcast information such as a vessel’s Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number, type, position, and course to nearby ships and coastal authorities. Despite its essential role, AIS is widely recognized to have significant limitations, including incomplete coverage and vulnerabilities to deliberate manipulation [ 5 ] . Spoofing AIS messages to falsify identity or location, as well as intentionally deactivating transmissions, referred to as “dark vessels”, are well-known tactics of manipulation. For example, in July 2023, a Malaysian-flagged oil tanker was found to have spoofed its AIS signals to mask its true location, a tactic used for loading and transferring Iranian oil in violation of US sanctions [ 6 ] . Similarly, in late 2024, the Finnish Coast Guard reported that tankers had spoofed their location data to conceal visits to Russian ports [ 7 ] . As such, recent technical advances have introduced space-based radio frequency (RF) detections as a promising complementary data source for vessel tracking. As integrating AIS and space-based RF data appears highly valuable, the use of statistical techniques for their data fusion should be explored. Therefore, the main research question behind this study is: How can AIS and RF data be matched to enhance ship identification? To address this question, this research proposes using a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM). The goal is to evaluate the potential of this statistical model for linking AIS data with space-based RF detections to improve vessel identification. III Related work Because of the inherent limitations of AIS, numerous studies have explored methods to detect falsified AIS messages [ 15 ] and to augment AIS with complementary data. A common approach involves combining AIS signals with satellite imagery, including optical data [ 16 ] and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) [ 17 , 18 ] . More recently, AIS has also been fused with radio frequency (RF) detections from both shore-based and space-based systems. Shore-based systems use radar stations that capture reflections of their own transmitted RF signals, while space-based systems rely on satellites that passively collect emissions from ships. Yang et al. [ 19 ] employed a graph matching-based deep neural network to align AIS data with shore-based radar tracks, whereas Zhang et al. [ 20 ] introduced a trajectory association method (D-TRAP) based on spatial proximity and directional consistency to improve matching robustness in multi-ship environments. The effectiveness of space-based RF systems has been demonstrated in case studies from UnseenLabs [ 21 ] and HawkEye 360 [ 22 ] , two commercial providers of satellite-based RF data. Although space-based RF has proven its practical value, its fusion with AIS remains a relatively new field of research. Initial studies by Yang et al. [ 23 , 24 ] applied linear interpolation and dead reckoning to temporally align AIS signals with RF detections. For this reason, this study focuses on the integration of AIS and space-based RF observations. While interpolation is straightforward to implement, representing the actual movements of ships, such as changes in course and speed or the intentional deactivation of AIS, is difficult. The longer the interval between AIS signals, the greater the potential error in the estimated positions [ 26 ] . For this reason, this study focuses on statistical methods by using a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to evaluate entire AIS trajectories, consisting of hundreds or thousands of signals, against individual RF detections using a probabilistic model. IV Data Understanding The goal of the Data Understanding phase of the CRISP-DM framework is to collect the relevant data and explore its quality and structure. Because commercial providers such as UnseenLabs and HawkEye 360 do not offer public access to RF data, we generate synthetic RF detections from AIS data, based on publicly documented characteristics of real RF systems (Section V ). The AIS dataset comes from NOAA’s Marine Cadastre [ 27 ] and contains transmissions from vessels operating along the United States coastline between 1 and 31 January 2024. It includes roughly 222 222 million AIS messages sent by 33,635 33{,}635 unique vessels, grouped into 83 83 vessel categories such as fishing, military, and cargo ships. Each AIS message contains identification fields (e.g., MMSI and IMO number), position, speed, and course. The presence of unique identifiers allows to group messages by vessel and reconstruct trajectories, defined as continuous sequences of AIS messages for a given ship between a start and end time. Pleasure crafts, yachts, and fishing vessels form the largest share of trajectories, but they mainly use Class B AIS transponders which transmit less frequently than Class A and lead to sparser and less accurate tracks ( 91 % 91\% of pleasure crafts, 75 % 75\% of fishing vessels). In contrast, 99 % 99\% of cargo vessels use Class A transponders. For this reason, the analysis focuses on cargo vessels, yielding 2,400 2{,}400 trajectories.
