First, more than 600 600 cargo vessels transmit between 5,000 5{,}000 and 10,000 10{,}000 messages per voyage, while a small group records fewer than five messages. This likely indicates incomplete records or very short trips. Second, the most frequently observed mean time interval between consecutive AIS messages falls between 150 150 and 180 180 seconds ( 2.5 2.5 - 3 3 minutes). This is longer than the nominal Class A reporting intervals ( 2 2 to 10 10 seconds underway, 3 3 minutes at anchor or moored), possibly due to resampling or limited reception. Many trajectories, however, contain mean intervals above 600 600 seconds ( 10 10 minutes), which can point to data quality issues, equipment problems, or deliberate AIS deactivation. Third, the vessel speeds, computed from the geographic distance and time between successive AIS messages, are for most cargo vessels between 5 5 and 20 20 km/h. This is plausible given the port and coastal segments in the data. A considerable share of the trajectories averages below 5 5 km/h and some contain very high speeds, so both groups merit closer inspection in later preprocessing. V Data preparation The Data Preparation stage involves cleaning and structuring of the AIS data as a time-ordered sequence suitable for use in a PHMM and generating synthetic RF data from the processed AIS dataset. V-A AIS Data Preprocessing Pipeline As the RF detections are generated synthetically and anchored to AIS tracks, the AIS data serves as ground truth for the matching task. Step 2: Removal of Speed Outliers The second step addresses outliers in vessel speed values. First, trajectories with unrealistically high-speed samples are removed using the interquartile range (IQR) method, with trajectories exceeding Q ​ 3 + 1.5 × ( Q ​ 3 − Q ​ 1 ) Q3+1.5\times(Q3-Q1) considered outliers. This aims to preserve trajectories exhibiting plausible movement patterns. The aim is to enhance continuity and minimize interruptions caused by extended periods without recorded positions. Each newly created segment is additionally subject to the same minimum-length (Step 1) and minimum-average-speed (Step 2) criteria. The segmentation increased the dataset size from 1,368 1,368 to 16,727 16,727 trajectories. Segments of the same vessel are treated as distinct candidates. Since the temporal preselection (Sec. VI-B ) requires a candidate to cover the RF timestamp, and segments split at gaps are disjoint in time, only 10 10 of 17,081 17,081 RF points have another segment of the true vessel in their candidate set, so this has a negligible effect on the reported precision. Step 1: Build Sampling Schedule First, a 24-hour sampling schedule is constructed to mimic the temporal characteristics of satellite observations. RF timestamps that fall within the extended window are then matched to the closest AIS message in time. Assuming that north- and east errors are uncorrelated and have the same variance, then the magnitude of the error follows a Rayleigh distribution. Today, an estimated 90 % 90\% of all international goods, ranging from raw materials to everyday products such as fruit and clothing, are transported by sea [ 1 ] . Maritime transport is attractive because vessels can carry large volumes of cargo over long distances at relatively low cost. However, the growing reliance on this mode of transportation, combined with other maritime traffic, has led to increased congestion at sea [ 2 ] . This is particularly evident near ports and in narrow waterways, where dense traffic heightens the risk of accidents. In addition to congestion, the vast and largely unregulated nature of the oceans facilitates illicit activities such as smuggling, unreported fishing, and sanctions evasion. Although initially designed as a collision-avoidance tool, authorities rely heavily on the Automatic Identification System (AIS) [ 3 , 4 ] for continuous vessel tracking. AIS transponders broadcast information such as a vessel’s Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number, type, position, and course to nearby ships and coastal authorities. Spoofing AIS messages to falsify identity or location, as well as intentionally deactivating transmissions, referred to as “dark vessels”, are well-known tactics of manipulation. For example, in July 2023, a Malaysian-flagged oil tanker was found to have spoofed its AIS signals to mask its true location, a tactic used for loading and transferring Iranian oil in violation of US sanctions [ 6 ] . Similarly, in late 2024, the Finnish Coast Guard reported that tankers had spoofed their location data to conceal visits to Russian ports [ 7 ] . As such, recent technical advances have introduced space-based radio frequency (RF) detections as a promising complementary data source for vessel tracking. An exploratory analysis of these cargo vessel trajectories produced three main insights. First, more than 600 600 cargo vessels transmit between 5,000 5{,}000 and 10,000 10{,}000 messages per voyage, while a small group records fewer than five messages. This likely indicates incomplete records or very short trips. Second, the most frequently observed mean time interval between consecutive AIS messages falls between 150 150 and 180 180 seconds ( 2.5 2.5 - 3 3 minutes). This is longer than the nominal Class A reporting intervals ( 2 2 to 10 10 seconds underway, 3 3 minutes at anchor or moored), possibly due to resampling or limited reception. Many trajectories, however, contain mean intervals above 600 600 seconds ( 10 10 minutes), which can point to data quality issues, equipment problems, or deliberate AIS deactivation. Third, the vessel speeds, computed from the geographic distance and time between successive AIS messages, are for most cargo vessels between 5 5 and 20 20 km/h. This is plausible given the port and coastal segments in the data. A considerable share of the trajectories averages below 5 5 km/h and some contain very high speeds, so both groups merit closer inspection in later preprocessing. It must therefore contain only plausible, continuously transmitted vessel behavior. Implausible kinematics or transmission gaps would make the ground-truth label of a synthetic RF point ambiguous, regardless of whether their underlying cause is a data-quality artifact or a dark vessel. The raw cargo AIS data ( 2,400 2,400 unique cargo trajectories) is accordingly preprocessed with a multi-step pipeline that removes such cases and structures the remaining data for sequence alignment. Four steps were applied. Step 1: Removal of Short Trajectories The first step is to remove trajectories with five or fewer AIS messages. The aim is to retain only trajectories with sufficient information value and a reasonable likelihood of temporal alignment with synthetic RF detections, which are typically acquired at relatively long intervals. In total, 80 80 trajectories were excluded, leaving 2,320 2,320 for subsequent filtering. As a result, the average number of AIS messages per trajectory increased by 3.45 % 3.45\% , rising from approximately 6,117 6,117 to 6,328 6,328 . Step 2: Removal of Speed Outliers The second step addresses outliers in vessel speed values. First, trajectories with unrealistically high-speed samples are removed using the interquartile range (IQR) method, with trajectories exceeding Q ​ 3 + 1.5 × ( Q ​ 3 − Q ​ 1 ) Q3+1.5\times(Q3-Q1) considered outliers. This aims to preserve trajectories exhibiting plausible movement patterns. Second, trajectories with an average speed below 5 5 km/h are removed, as they are assumed to represent stationary vessels not considered in this study. The majority of cargo vessels maintained average speeds between 7 7 and 20 20 km/h, with a mean of 14.03 14.03 km/h. Only a few trajectories exhibited average speeds above 35 35 km/h, with a maximum of 40 40 km/h, which still is a plausible operating speed under certain conditions [ 28 ] . Trajectories containing gaps longer than 551 seconds (approximately nine minutes, corresponding to the 99 99 th percentile of all inter-message time gaps pooled across the Step 2 output) are segmented into shorter trajectories. The aim is to enhance continuity and minimize interruptions caused by extended periods without recorded positions. Each newly created segment is additionally subject to the same minimum-length (Step 1) and minimum-average-speed (Step 2) criteria. The segmentation increased the dataset size from 1,368 1,368 to 16,727 16,727 trajectories. Segments of the same vessel are treated as distinct candidates. Since the temporal preselection (Sec. VI-B ) requires a candidate to cover the RF timestamp, and segments split at gaps are disjoint in time, only 10 10 of 17,081 17,081 RF points have another segment of the true vessel in their candidate set, so this has a negligible effect on the reported precision. This step aims to reduce computational time by creating a smaller yet representative dataset while preserving trajectory diversity. To this end, a sample of 5,000 5,000 trajectories is selected using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE). Rather than uniform random sampling, KDE assigns selection probabilities based on selected features of an AIS track (total number of AIS messages, voyage duration, average speed, geographical displacement latitude and longitude, average time interval between consecutive messages). This ensures a balance between common and rare trajectory patterns. Each trajectory in this sample is then converted into a sequence of tuples ( timestamp UTC , ( latitude , longitude ) ) (\texttt{timestamp}_{\texttt{UTC}},(\texttt{latitude},\texttt{longitude})) and ordered chronologically to maintain temporal consistency. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.18553 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Nov 2026] Title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers Authors: Aayush Marasini , Barsat Khadka , Nick Rahimi View a PDF of the paper titled WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers, by Aayush Marasini and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at this https URL . Comments: 9 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. items.content: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers Aayush Marasini Affiliation: The University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS 39401, USA Barsat Khadka Affiliation: The University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS 39401, USA Correspondence to: Barsat.Khadka@usm.edu Nick Rahimi Affiliation: The University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS 39401, USA Abstract Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH , a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2 ​ K 2K -parameter control policies to 7 ​ B 7B -parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus’s 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench . Keywords: Weight-Space Programming, Large Language Models, Neural Network Editing, Benchmarking † † affiliationnotice: Equal contribution 1 Introduction Traditionally, neural networks are developed by specifying an architecture and learning its parameters through optimization. Once trained, these weights are generally treated as the output of the learning process rather than something that can be read or programmed directly. However, previous work on model editing has shown that specific behaviors can be changed through targeted modifications to network weights ( Meng et al., 2022 ) , while compilers such as Tracr have demonstrated that Transformer weights can be constructed directly from symbolic programs ( Lindner et al., 2023 ) . More recently, Takehi et al. (2026) demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can perform a broader range of operations on neural network weights themselves. They showed that LLMs can identify what a network was trained to do, repair failures by modifying its parameters, and construct working networks from scratch without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP), drawing an analogy to traditional programming, but operating directly on neural network weights rather than source code. Although these demonstrations show that WSP is possible, they do not yet establish how reliably LLMs can perform these operations across different networks and tasks. For instance, identifying the behavior of a small control policy is different from locating learned behaviors in a large language model, and successfully repairing one failure does not necessarily mean that other capabilities are preserved. It is also unclear how these abilities change with the capability of the LLM performing the weight-space operations. Understanding these differences requires a systematic evaluation across network architectures, model sizes, and task difficulties. Evaluating WSP also presents challenges that are not typically encountered in conventional language model benchmarks. An agent may inspect weight tensors, analyze them using numerical tools, or execute the network to observe its behavior. These forms of access are not equivalent. With unrestricted forward passes, an agent could discover successful edits through repeated trial and error rather than reasoning about the weights. Furthermore, an edit that improves a target behavior may degrade unrelated capabilities, while some requested modifications may be infeasible under the given constraints. A meaningful evaluation must therefore control how agents access and execute networks, while measuring both the intended improvements and their costs. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce WEIGHTBENCH , a benchmark for evaluating LLMs as weight-space programmers. WEIGHTBENCH defines 42 task specifications across five tracks: reading weights, repairing networks, constructing networks from scratch, recognizing infeasible modifications, and data-free compression. The tasks span networks ranging from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. We evaluate agents under explicit access and compute constraints, with task-specific scoring that accounts for performance improvements, unintended behavioral changes, and the costs of modifications. Non-agentic baselines and reference solutions are included to establish task difficulty and measure the available room for improvement. 2 Background 2.1 Weight-Space Programming Weight-Space Programming (WSP), introduced by Takehi et al. (2026) , investigates whether general-purpose LLMs can directly analyze and manipulate the parameters of neural networks. Rather than relying on a fixed editing algorithm, an agent examines the weights, performs numerical analysis when needed, and determines how to modify or construct the network. The initial demonstrations include identifying the tasks of trained networks, repairing failing policies, and constructing game-playing networks without gradient descent. Importantly, these experiments involve different levels of access, ranging from raw weights alone to code-assisted analysis and limited behavioral feedback. 2.2 Weight-Space Learning Weight-Space Learning (WSL) is a broader research direction that treats neural network parameters as structured data that can be analyzed, represented, and generated. Han et al. (2026) categorize WSL into three areas: weight-space understanding, representation, and generation. Weight-space understanding studies properties such as parameter symmetries, where different weight configurations can represent the same function. Weight-space representation learns useful features from model parameters, with methods such as Deep Weight-Space Networks ( Navon et al., 2023 ) and Neural Functional Networks ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) accounting for neuron permutation symmetries. Weight-space generation extends this idea to constructing model parameters through hypernetworks ( Ha et al., 2017 ) and generative models such as HyperDiffusion ( Erkoç et al., 2023 ) . While WSL develops specialized methods for understanding and generating weights, WSP investigates whether general-purpose LLMs can perform such operations through reasoning and tool use. 2.3 LLM Agent Benchmarks Recent benchmarks evaluate LLM agents on tasks requiring tool use, code execution, and multi-step problem solving. SWE-bench ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) evaluates software issue resolution, MLE-bench ( Chan et al., 2025 ) examines machine learning engineering, and PaperBench ( Starace et al., 2025 ) evaluates the replication of published research. These benchmarks measure agents through executable artifacts and task-specific evaluation criteria. Evaluating WSP introduces additional constraints, as unrestricted model execution or optimization can make it difficult to distinguish weight-level analysis from behavioral search. WeightBench builds on artifact-based agent evaluation while focusing specifically on operations performed on neural network parameters. 3 Evaluation Framework 3.1 Execution Environment and Auditing The main constraint of WSP is that modifications must be done from geometric or topological analysis of the neural network weights, not iterative or output-driven optimization. A naive evaluation framework is vulnerable to agents silently running gradient descent or unmetered froward passes to find solutions using train-and-error. To mitigate this, WeightBench boundes and observes an agent’s access, compute and edits, and scores every task under a strict budget. It executes all tasks within a strict, unprivilated OS-level sandbox. The agent is completely isolated from the host filesystem except for the task’s public artifacts and its workdir, and is denied access to model execution libraries (such as transformers or vllm ), and held in a strict network lockdown where the only exits are its own LLM API and the local, token-authenticated Weight API. We cannot enforce a zero forward pass constraint ( N f ​ o ​ r ​ w ​ a ​ r ​ d = 0 N_{f}orward=0 ) with a naive FLOP cap. Allowed analysis, such as computing the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of weight matrices, routinely costs more FLOPs than a forward pass. Therefore, WeightBench injects a metered NumPy subclass into every agent process and traces arithmetic on weights at the operator level. From these traces, our runtime guard detects forward-pas chains and records the violation. To guarantee the integrity of the evaluation, every metered forward pass, probe and runtime-guard event is recorded in a hash-chained ledger. If an agent tries to bypass the runtime guards, the system flags it and quarantines the run. The quarantined run scores 0 0 until a human review clears it. The final scores are computed directly from this ledger rather than the agent’s outputs. Thus we never have to trust the agent’s self reported work and making every submitted result verifiable. Figure 1: The WeightBench evaluation pipeline. 3.2 Evaluation Metrics To properly evaluate an agent’s ability to edit weights, we cannot just look at whether it solved the problem. A successful edit must improve the target capability while minimizing the edit’s footprint and computational overhead. It must also do so without causing catastrophic degradation of other capabilities of the neural network. Therefore, WeightBench evaluates the agent using a composite score, S W ​ B ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] S_{WB}\in[0,1] , defined by four components: • Task Gain ( S + ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] ) (S^{+}\in[0,1]) measures if the agent did the job. It tracks accuracy for tasks involving reading the weights, and for tasks involving diagnosis, the metric calculates how much the agent improved over the base model, divided by the total ”room for improvement” available between the base model and the absolute ceiling. • Collateral Damage ( D c ​ o ​ l ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] ) (D_{col}\in[0,1]) : quantifies the degradation of other capabilities caused by the weight edits. It is defined as the performance drop of the edited mode on held-out benchmarks (e.g., MMLU). It is lower bounded at 0 0 to ensure that accidental improvements do not offset performance losses elsewhere. • Structural Edit Cost ( u edit ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] u_{\text{edit}}\in[0,1] ): evaluates how precise and surgical the agent’s weight changes are. For tasks that don’t use an edit budget (like reading or building from scratch), we set u edit = 0 u_{\text{edit}}=0 . For tasks that do, it tracks the size of the update using the smaller of the L 0 L_{0} parameter count fraction and the matrix rank fraction. If a submission blows past either budget limit, it gets disqualified ( 0 0 ). Ultimately, this metric penalizes broad, messy edits and rewards clean, targeted fixes. • Compute Use ( E / E b ​ u ​ d ​ g ​ e ​ t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] ) (E/E_{budget}\in[0,1]) accounts for the computational resources expended. It is measured as the ratio of metered diagnostic probes and forward passes used relative to the task’s budget. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH , a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2 ​ K 2K -parameter control policies to 7 ​ B 7B -parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. Once trained, these weights are generally treated as the output of the learning process rather than something that can be read or programmed directly. However, previous work on model editing has shown that specific behaviors can be changed through targeted modifications to network weights ( Meng et al., 2022 ) , while compilers such as Tracr have demonstrated that Transformer weights can be constructed directly from symbolic programs ( Lindner et al., 2023 ) . More recently, Takehi et al. (2026) demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can perform a broader range of operations on neural network weights themselves. They showed that LLMs can identify what a network was trained to do, repair failures by modifying its parameters, and construct working networks from scratch without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP), drawing an analogy to traditional programming, but operating directly on neural network weights rather than source code. Although these demonstrations show that WSP is possible, they do not yet establish how reliably LLMs can perform these operations across different networks and tasks. For instance, identifying the behavior of a small control policy is different from locating learned behaviors in a large language model, and successfully repairing one failure does not necessarily mean that other capabilities are preserved. It is also unclear how these abilities change with the capability of the LLM performing the weight-space operations. Understanding these differences requires a systematic evaluation across network architectures, model sizes, and task difficulties. Evaluating WSP also presents challenges that are not typically encountered in conventional language model benchmarks. An agent may inspect weight tensors, analyze them using numerical tools, or execute the network to observe its behavior. These forms of access are not equivalent. With unrestricted forward passes, an agent could discover successful edits through repeated trial and error rather than reasoning about the weights. Furthermore, an edit that improves a target behavior may degrade unrelated capabilities, while some requested modifications may be infeasible under the given constraints. A meaningful evaluation must therefore control how agents access and execute networks, while measuring both the intended improvements and their costs. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce WEIGHTBENCH , a benchmark for evaluating LLMs as weight-space programmers. WEIGHTBENCH defines 42 task specifications across five tracks: reading weights, repairing networks, constructing networks from scratch, recognizing infeasible modifications, and data-free compression. The tasks span networks ranging from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. We evaluate agents under explicit access and compute constraints, with task-specific scoring that accounts for performance improvements, unintended behavioral changes, and the costs of modifications. Non-agentic baselines and reference solutions are included to establish task difficulty and measure the available room for improvement. 2 Background 2.1 Weight-Space Programming Weight-Space Programming (WSP), introduced by Takehi et al. (2026) , investigates whether general-purpose LLMs can directly analyze and manipulate the parameters of neural networks. Rather than relying on a fixed editing algorithm, an agent examines the weights, performs numerical analysis when needed, and determines how to modify or construct the network. The initial demonstrations include identifying the tasks of trained networks, repairing failing policies, and constructing game-playing networks without gradient descent. Importantly, these experiments involve different levels of access, ranging from raw weights alone to code-assisted analysis and limited behavioral feedback. 2.2 Weight-Space Learning Weight-Space Learning (WSL) is a broader research direction that treats neural network parameters as structured data that can be analyzed, represented, and generated. Han et al. (2026) categorize WSL into three areas: weight-space understanding, representation, and generation. Weight-space understanding studies properties such as parameter symmetries, where different weight configurations can represent the same function. Weight-space representation learns useful features from model parameters, with methods such as Deep Weight-Space Networks ( Navon et al., 2023 ) and Neural Functional Networks ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) accounting for neuron permutation symmetries. Weight-space generation extends this idea to constructing model parameters through hypernetworks ( Ha et al., 2017 ) and generative models such as HyperDiffusion ( Erkoç et al., 2023 ) . While WSL develops specialized methods for understanding and generating weights, WSP investigates whether general-purpose LLMs can perform such operations through reasoning and tool use. 2.3 LLM Agent Benchmarks Recent benchmarks evaluate LLM agents on tasks requiring tool use, code execution, and multi-step problem solving. These benchmarks measure agents through executable artifacts and task-specific evaluation criteria. Evaluating WSP introduces additional constraints, as unrestricted model execution or optimization can make it difficult to distinguish weight-level analysis from behavioral search. items.content:
On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions Brandon Amos Affiliation: Reflection AI Email: brandon@reflection.ai Abstract Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests. 1 Introduction Standard implementations of the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss subtract the maximum logit to avoid overflow, but their gradients can still suffer from rounding and cancellation. Barron et al. (2026) analyze and fix two such issues. First, softmax collapse , previously identified by Prieto et al. (2025) , occurs for confident hard-target predictions. The target probability rounds to one, making its cross-entropy gradient zero even though the other categories retain positive probabilities and nonzero gradients. Retaining the small probability tail avoids this failure. Second, softmax cancellation affects soft cross-entropy when the prediction and target distributions are nearly equal. The gradient depends on small differences between their probabilities, which separate normalization and rounding can erase. Computed target probabilities need not sum exactly to one, so differentiation can even produce a nonzero gradient for identical logits. Reconstructing probability differences from logit differences, together with a zero-sum correction, addresses this second failure. These results motivate further studying numerical accuracy in divergences. The forward KL inherits the soft cross-entropy gradient issue because their gradients coincide when the reference distribution is fixed. Divergences themselves also vanish as the distributions approach equality, so their forward computations can suffer cancellation as well. Applications potentially affected by these errors include knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal optimization, where these quantities serve as fitting terms and regularizers. Section 2 expands on these. Contributions of this paper. For nearly equal distributions, we identify five numerical issues in standard implementations of the forward and gradient computations of 1) the forward and reverse KL divergences, including Monte Carlo KL estimators and entropy penalties ( section 4 ), and 2) the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence ( section 5 ). To address these issues, we cover eight reformulations and provide executable JAX examples validated by property-based tests. Table 1 summarizes the settings. Does it matter in practice? The examples isolate the arithmetic rather than measure large-scale training outcomes. Section 3 further discusses their practical significance. Table 1: Numerical issues for nearly equal (categorical) distributions. Setting Forward issue Gradient issue Forward KL ( section 4.1 ) KL-sum cancellation Softmax subtraction Reverse KL ( section 4.2 ) KL-sum cancellation Log-softmax subtraction Entropy via reverse KL to uniform ( section 4.2.1 ) No issue present Log-probability centering Monte Carlo K1: log-ratio ( section 4.3.3 ) Log-softmax subtraction No issue present Monte Carlo K2: squared log-ratio ( section 4.3.4 ) Log-softmax subtraction Inherits forward issue Monte Carlo K3: control variate ( section 4.3.5 ) Remainder cancellation Rounded exponential Generalized JSD ( section 5 ) KL-sum cancellation Mixture log-ratio rounding Mixture log-ratio rounding Notation and setup. Because this is an ML paper, we consider a model f θ f_{	heta} with parameters θ 	heta that maps an input x x to logits z = f θ ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ K z=f_{	heta}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{K} over K K categories (e.g., vocabulary entries), although our main analysis here only considers the logits regardless of how they were obtained. The logits define a categorical distribution q = softmax ⁡ ( z ) q=\operatorname{softmax}(z) , and p = softmax ⁡ ( z ref ) p=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{\mathrm{ref}}) is a fixed reference distribution with logits z ref ∈ ℝ K z_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} , potentially also generated by another model. We analyze the forward computation of each divergence and its gradient with respect to z z . Gradients with respect to θ 	heta follow by the chain rule. Appendix A gives further details on the numerical conventions, experimental protocol, and helper implementations. 2 Applications of optimizing divergences Divergences appear in many optimization objectives, both as fitting terms and as regularizers. The consequences of numerical error depend on the weight of the divergence term and how its gradient propagates through the model and optimizer. Knowledge distillation and on-policy distillation. Knowledge distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s predictions ( Buciluă et al., 2006 ; Hinton et al., 2015 ; Kim & Rush, 2016 ) , with on-policy variants using student-generated contexts ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . A student with parameters θ 	heta predicts q θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) q_{	heta}(\cdot\mid x) at context x x . The context distribution μ \mu comes from data or student rollouts and is held fixed during each update. The objective compares the student’s predictions with a fixed teacher p ( ⋅ ∣ x ) p(\cdot\mid x) : min θ 𝔼 x ∼ μ [ D ( p ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , q θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ) ] , \min_{	heta}\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu}\left[D igl(p(\cdot\mid x),q_{	heta}(\cdot\mid x) igr)ight], (1) where D D is a divergence commonly chosen as the forward KL, reverse KL, or generalized JSD, as in Agarwal et al. (2024, Section 4.1) . Here, the numerical issues discussed in this paper can arise near optimality as the student’s predictions approach the teacher’s. Reinforcement learning with reverse-KL or entropy regularization. A policy with parameters θ 	heta generates outputs y ∼ π θ y\sim\pi_{	heta} . With penalty weight λ > 0 \lambda>0 , the objective balances reward r ⁡ ( y ) r(y) against a reverse-KL penalty that encourages the policy to remain close to a fixed reference policy π ref \pi_{m ref} : max θ 𝔼 y ∼ π θ [ r ( y ) ] − λ KL ( π θ ∥ π ref ) . \max_{	heta}\ \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{	heta}}[r(y)]-\lambda\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{	heta}\parallel\pi_{m ref}). (2) Reverse-KL penalties regularize control and policy optimization ( Todorov, 2006 ; Geist et al., 2019 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . The numerical issues discussed in this paper can arise when the policy is close to its reference. Entropy bonuses encourage exploration ( Williams & Peng, 1991 ; Mnih et al., 2016 ) . For a categorical policy, maximizing entropy is equivalent to penalizing the reverse KL to the uniform distribution. Similarly, entropy gradients can become inaccurate near a uniform policy. These errors may have limited practical impact when the task favors nonuniform behavior or behavior far from the reference policy. In these cases, the gradient may be dominated by that of the expected reward. Proximal optimization with reverse KL. Proximal methods can minimize a base objective F F with a reverse-KL penalty that discourages large changes from the current distribution q θ k q_{	heta_{k}} , which remains fixed during each update ( Teboulle, 1992 ) : θ k + 1 ∈ arg min θ { F ( θ ) + η k − 1 KL ( q θ ∥ q θ k ) } , η k > 0 . 	heta_{k+1}\in\arg\min_{	heta}\left\{F(	heta)+\eta_{k}^{-1}\operatorname{KL}(q_{	heta}\parallel q_{	heta_{k}})ight\},\qquad\eta_{k}>0. (3) Reverse-KL regularization of successive iterates also motivates natural-gradient methods ( Amari, 1998 ; Martens, 2020 ) . Related policy-search methods constrain the KL between successive policies ( Peters et al., 2010 ; Schulman et al., 2015 ) . The numerical issues discussed in this paper can arise when successive distributions are nearly equal, although the gradient may be dominated by that of F F . 3 Discussion on the scope and practical significance Before developing the reformulations, we discuss where they apply and how to interpret their numerical accuracy in optimization. When to use the reformulations. Some reformulations also require nearly equal distributions and may be numerically unstable outside this regime. Full production implementations are outside the scope of this paper, but we indicate where guards and fallback evaluations are needed. For example, the soft cross-entropy implementation of Barron et al. (2026) uses the correction only for log-ratios with magnitude below one and switches to direct probability subtraction otherwise. Section 4.1.1 illustrates this limitation for forward KL: although the reformulation is algebraically valid, its intermediate computations can overflow away from equality. The same limitation applies to other reformulations that share this log-ratio reconstruction. Numerical issues are exacerbated at lower precision. Our examples use FP32. Barron et al. (2026, Section 7) compare BF16, FP32, and FP64 in soft-target distillation and observe larger residual gradient errors and parameter drift in BF16. Lower precision can make rounding dominate at larger separations between distributions, when the divergence and its gradient are larger. Other lower-precision formats, such as FP8 and FP4, could make these issues even more prevalent when used to compute divergences and their gradients. At higher precision, large relative errors may still have very small absolute magnitude. Adam’s stabilizing constant. Barron et al. (2026, Sections 5 and 7) study how the stabilizing constant ϵ \epsilon in Adam ( Kingma & Ba, 2015 ) limits the amplification of small gradients. Our examples examine numerical accuracy without measuring its effects on training. In their soft-target distillation experiment, Adam amplifies rounding residuals and moves a student away from an initially identical teacher. The divergences considered here raise a similar concern: their true gradients vanish at equality, but numerical errors can produce nonzero updates. The practical effect depends on the parameter-gradient statistics used by Adam, after backpropagation through the model and combination with other objective terms. Remaining rounding errors. Accuracy also depends on normalization, reductions, and input storage. A reformulation cannot recover a displacement already rounded away in its inputs. Compensated summation can retain rounding residuals in the sampled log-ratio ( reformulation 5 ), improving accuracy when its two differences nearly cancel ( Ogita et al., 2005 , Sections 3–4) . This costs additional arithmetic and cannot correct errors already present in the supplied log-normalizers. 4 Fixing Kullback–Leibler divergences From the setup, p = softmax ⁡ ( z ref ) p=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{\mathrm{ref}}) is the fixed categorical reference and q = softmax ⁡ ( z ) q=\operatorname{softmax}(z) is the distribution being optimized. The forward and reverse KL are defined as: Definition 1 (Forward KL) . KL ( p ∥ q ) \displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(p\parallel q) = 𝔼 a ∼ p ​ [ log ⁡ p a − log ⁡ q a ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}[\log p_{a}-\log q_{a}] (4) = ∑ i p i ​ ( log ⁡ p i − log ⁡ q i ) . \displaystyle\mathrel{\color[rgb]{0.45,0.45,0.45}=}{\color[rgb]{0.45,0.45,0.45}\sum_{i}p_{i}(\log p_{i}-\log q_{i})}. Definition 2 (Reverse KL) . KL ( q ∥ p ) \displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(q\parallel p) = 𝔼 a ∼ q ​ [ log ⁡ q a − log ⁡ p a ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q}[\log q_{a}-\log p_{a}] (5) = ∑ i q i ​ ( log ⁡ q i − log ⁡ p i ) . \displaystyle\mathrel{\color[rgb]{0.45,0.45,0.45}=}{\color[rgb]{0.45,0.45,0.45}\sum_{i}q_{i}(\log q_{i}-\log p_{i})}. On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions Brandon Amos Affiliation: Reflection AI Email: brandon@reflection.ai Abstract Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests. 1 Introduction Standard implementations of the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss subtract the maximum logit to avoid overflow, but their gradients can still suffer from rounding and cancellation. Barron et al. (2026) analyze and fix two such issues. First, softmax collapse , previously identified by Prieto et al. (2025) , occurs for confident hard-target predictions. The target probability rounds to one, making its cross-entropy gradient zero even though the other categories retain positive probabilities and nonzero gradients. Retaining the small probability tail avoids this failure. Second, softmax cancellation affects soft cross-entropy when the prediction and target distributions are nearly equal. The gradient depends on small differences between their probabilities, which separate normalization and rounding can erase. Computed target probabilities need not sum exactly to one, so differentiation can even produce a nonzero gradient for identical logits. Reconstructing probability differences from logit differences, together with a zero-sum correction, addresses this second failure. These results motivate further studying numerical accuracy in divergences. The forward KL inherits the soft cross-entropy gradient issue because their gradients coincide when the reference distribution is fixed. Divergences themselves also vanish as the distributions approach equality, so their forward computations can suffer cancellation as well. Applications potentially affected by these errors include knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal optimization, where these quantities serve as fitting terms and regularizers. Section 2 expands on these. Contributions of this paper. For nearly equal distributions, we identify five numerical issues in standard implementations of the forward and gradient computations of 1) the forward and reverse KL divergences, including Monte Carlo KL estimators and entropy penalties ( section 4 ), and 2) the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence ( section 5 ). To address these issues, we cover eight reformulations and provide executable JAX examples validated by property-based tests. Table 1 summarizes the settings. Does it matter in practice? The examples isolate the arithmetic rather than measure large-scale training outcomes. Section 3 further discusses their practical significance. (2026, Section 7) compare BF16, FP32, and FP64 in soft-target distillation and observe larger residual gradient errors and parameter drift in BF16. (2026, Sections 5 and 7) study how the stabilizing constant ϵ \epsilon in Adam ( Kingma & Ba, 2015 ) limits the amplification of small gradients. Accuracy also depends on normalization, reductions, and input storage. A reformulation cannot recover a displacement already rounded away in its inputs. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.18507 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Nov 2026] Title: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy Authors: Omer Nezih Gerek View a PDF of the paper titled Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy, by Omer Nezih Gerek View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts. Comments: 22 pages, 2 figures. Companion paper: to be uploaded. Zhang , Connor Mattson , Daniel S. Brown View a PDF of the paper titled Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, by Tony H. Zhang and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline. Comments: 9 pages, 5 figures. items.content: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning 3029 Tony H. Zhang Note: Authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: University of Utah , SLC, UT , USA email: tony.h.zhang@utah.edu , Connor Mattson Affiliation: University of Utah , SLC, UT , USA email: c.mattson@utah.edu and Daniel S. Brown Affiliation: University of Utah , SLC, UT , USA email: daniel.s.brown@utah.edu 2027 Abstract. Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies 2.6 2.6 – 4.2 × 4.2\times faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline. Code, rollout videos and full results are available at https://zhanghutony.github.io/ibmarl/ . Keywords: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, Learning from Demonstration, Imitation Learning, Human-in-the-loop Learning 1. Introduction Cooperative multi-agent tasks are difficult for Reinforcement Learning (RL) to solve: the joint-action space grows exponentially with the number of agents, credit assignment across agents is ambiguous, and rewards are often inherently sparse ( Albrecht et al., 2024 ) . Even with a known model, finding an optimal joint policy for a finite-horizon Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) is NEXP-complete ( Bernstein et al., 2002 ) , so a learner that must also discover the reward through random joint exploration faces a search that grows with every agent added. In single-agent RL, demonstrations have been shown to help with this exploration problem, as examples of good behavior can often lead agents toward a reward signal even in sparse-reward tasks. Methods such as DQfD ( Hester et al., 2018 ) , DDPGfD ( Vecerik et al., 2017 ) , and DDPG + BC ( Nair et al., 2018 ) seed the replay buffer or regularize the learner toward expert data, and Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) ( Hu et al., 2024 ) goes further by keeping a behavior-cloned policy in the loop, using it to propose actions during exploration and to improve the bootstrap target (Sec. 3.1 ). Figure 1. IBMARL overview. (1) Teach: a human teleoperates one robot at a time while the others run their current IL policies (R2BC), producing a frozen IL policy for each robot. (2) Act: each robot’s IL and RL policies propose an action, and the centralized critic ensembles choose, per robot, which one the team executes. (3) Learn: the experience trains the critics, and each RL policy is pulled toward its IL action only where the critics prefer it. At deployment, each robot runs its RL policy alone. We address two obstacles that block the extension of such frameworks to MARL: (i) Demonstrations. Nearly all multi-agent imitation learning (MAIL) assumes joint demonstrations, in which an expert must simultaneously command all N N agents—data a lone human operator cannot realistically provide for collaborating teams ( Mattson et al., 2026 ; Turco et al., 2024 ) . To address this, we leverage Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) ( Mattson et al., 2026 ) (Sec. 3.2 ), which has the demonstrator cycle through controlling each agent of the team, while the other agents execute their current learned policies, yielding decentralized cooperative policies from realistic single-human demonstrations. However, R2BC inherits the limitations of behavior cloning: covariate shift, a performance ceiling at the demonstrator, and a prohibitive demonstration burden for the last increments of task performance. (ii) Decentralized execution. IBRL’s deployed policy relies on the critic at every step to choose between the IL action and the RL action. For a team, a critic that judges joint actions must have access to every agent’s observation and action, so keeping it during deployment would require centralized execution or communication. To avoid this, the RL actors must be deployable on their own, but nothing in IBRL ensures that they are, and the RL policies lag behind the policy that was actually executed during training (Sec. 6.3 ). We address both obstacles with Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL) , which keeps the R2BC policy in the loop rather than only in the data (Fig. 1 ). Assuming access to a task reward, we ask: Can MARL be bootstrapped from policies trained from realistic single-agent demonstrations, and can the result be deployed without the critics? During training (Fig. 1 , Act), every agent receives one action from its imitation policy and one from its RL actor, and centralized critic ensembles choose, per agent, which to execute. The same choice is made inside the TD target, so the critics learn the value of the better of the two policies rather than of the RL actors alone. RL thus improves on the R2BC policy where it is wrong while still following it where it is right, so the demonstrator’s ceiling of (i) is not inherited. For (ii), the critics’ preference also sets, state by state, how strongly each policy is pulled toward its imitation action (Fig. 1 , Learn), so the actors converge to the policy the critics execute and can be deployed alone, without the critics or the imitation policy. The contributions of this work are: (i) We formulate IBMARL , a generalization of IBRL to cooperative Dec-POMDPs in which the imitation-learned (IL) policy is a set of N N decentralized R2BC policies and a centralized critic ensemble arbitrates among per-agent combinations of IL and RL proposals. (ii) We introduce a gated imitation penalty that pulls each RL policy toward the IL proposal in proportion to the critics’ preference for it, so that the actors alone match the centralized policy and execution is decentralized. (iii) We evaluate IBMARL on four cooperative tasks in VMAS ( Bettini et al., 2022 ) using synthetic demonstrators. Here, IBMARL surpasses the IL policies 2.6 2.6 – 4.2 × 4.2\times faster than demonstration-based baselines on Navigation and 2.8 × 2.8\times faster on the physically coupled Buzzwire task, is the only method to surpass the IL policies on Balance and Transport, and exceeds the performance of the demonstrator on Buzzwire and Balance. (iv) We evaluate IBMARL with a real human operator using R2BC’s round-robin interface on Buzzwire, where IBMARL surpasses the human-trained IL policy more than twice as fast as the best baseline, suggesting that the gains carry over from synthetic to real demonstrators. 2. Related Work Single-Agent RL with Demonstrations: A significant body of prior work combines expert demonstrations with single-agent RL. In the simplest instantiation, offline demonstrations pretrain the starting policy by behavior cloning ( Ankile et al., 2025 ; Ramrakhya et al., 2023 ; Rajeswaran et al., 2018 ) or, for off-policy methods, populate the replay buffer with the demonstrated transitions ( Hester et al., 2018 ; Nair et al., 2020 ) . Both remove much of the early random exploration and give the critic high-value transitions from the start, which stabilizes early training and raises early returns over RL alone ( Rajeswaran et al., 2018 ; Hester et al., 2018 ; Kang et al., 2018 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) . A second family treats the demonstrations as offline data and adds a surrogate loss that keeps the policy or critic close to the demonstrated actions: DQfD’s large-margin term on the Double DQN loss ( Hester et al., 2018 ; Van Hasselt et al., 2016 ) , which surpasses both imitation and RL alone in nearly all of 42 Atari games within a million steps, and similar extensions in DDPGfD ( Vecerik et al., 2017 ) , POfD ( Kang et al., 2018 ) , NAC ( Gao et al., 2018 ) , Hybrid RL ( Song et al., 2023 ) and TD3+BC ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ) . When the reward is sparse, the demonstrations provide the signal: Nair et al. ( Nair et al., 2018 ) add a behavior-cloning loss to the DDPG policy and, for suboptimal demonstrations, gate it with a Q-filter so that it applies only where the critic rates the demonstrated action above the actor’s. IBRL ( Hu et al., 2024 ) keeps the imitation policy itself in the loop, letting the critic choose between its proposal and the actor’s at every step (Sec. 3.1 ). We propose IBMARL, the multi-agent generalization of IBRL; its gated imitation penalty is a soft, state-wise Q-filter applied to the IL policy’s action on the states the learner visits rather than to stored demonstrations. Multi-Agent RL with Demonstrations: Compared to the single-agent literature, MARL extensions that utilize demonstrations are few. Alagha et al. ( Alagha et al., 2023 ) let a synthetic expert take control of one agent during interaction so that part of the replay buffer is expert-provided, which improves early team performance; PRIMAL ( Sartoretti et al., 2019 ) trains decentralized policies by combining RL with imitation of a centralized planner; others reformulate particular MARL algorithms around demonstrations, namely MADDPG from demonstrations ( Qiu et al., 2023 ) , skill learning from demonstrations ( Venkatesh and Min, 2024 ) and hybrid training ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) ; a separate line imitates opponents in competitive games ( Bui et al., 2024 ) . The “-fD” regularizers above could in principle be added to QMIX ( Rashid et al., 2018 ) , VDN ( Sunehag et al., 2018 ) , FACMAC ( Peng et al., 2021 ) or LIIR ( Du et al., 2019 ) , but to our knowledge MADDPG from demonstrations ( Qiu et al., 2023 ) is the only work that has done so. By far the most relevant prior work is PegMARL ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , which also avoids joint demonstrations: single-agent demonstrations, given with no other agents present , train a behavioral discriminator and a transition discriminator that shape the sparse team reward online, leaving all teaching of cooperation to the reward. IBMARL differs in three ways. Its demonstrations are given through R2BC in the presence of teammates, so the IL policy already encodes cooperation; the IL policy acts through action proposals, bootstrap targets and a critic-gated pull on the policy rather than through reward shaping or a scheduled cloning penalty ( Nair et al., 2018 ; Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ) ; and the output is a set of decentralized actors that need neither the centralized critics nor the IL policy at run time. 3. Background IBMARL combines IBRL, which utilizes an imitation policy with RL, with R2BC, which makes a cooperative imitation policy obtainable for multi-agent systems from one human demonstrator. 3.1. Imitation Bootstrapped RL Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) ( Hu et al., 2024 ) is a single-agent off-policy actor-critic method that starts from a behavior-cloned IL policy μ ψ \mu_{\psi} , pretrained on a small set of demonstrations 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , and keeps it in the loop in two places. When acting, both policies propose an action for the current observation o o and the target critic Q ¯ ϕ \bar{Q}_{\phi} picks the better one, (1) a = arg ​ max a ′ ∈ { μ ψ ​ ( o ) , π θ ​ ( o ) } ⁡ Q ¯ ϕ ​ ( o , a ′ ) , a=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a^{\prime}\in\{\mu_{\psi}(o),\,\pi_{\theta}(o)\}}\bar{Q}_{\phi}(o,a^{\prime}), so early exploration follows the IL policy wherever the critic has found nothing better. The same choice is made at the next observation inside the TD target, (2) y = r + γ ​ max a ′ ∈ { μ ψ ​ ( o ′ ) , π ¯ θ ​ ( o ′ ) } ​ Q ¯ ϕ ​ ( o ′ , a ′ ) , y=r+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\{\mu_{\psi}(o^{\prime}),\,\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(o^{\prime})\}}\bar{Q}_{\phi}(o^{\prime},a^{\prime}), so the critic estimates the value of the better of the two policies and value propagates from states the IL policy can reach before the policy can. The replay buffer is pre-loaded with 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , and the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} is trained with the ordinary deterministic policy gradient on Q ϕ Q_{\phi} . With 10–50 demonstrations and a poor IL policy, IBRL reaches 85–100% success on real-robot manipulation tasks. Two features matter for what follows. First, the IL policy only ever supplies an action for the critic to pick or reject; it never enters the actor’s loss, so the policy itself is not trained toward it. Second, the propose-and-select step is also used at test time, so that the critic and IL policies are required for deployment. 3.2. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) ( Mattson et al., 2026 ) is an online multi-agent imitation learning method that learns a cooperative policy for N N agents from one demonstrator who controls a single agent at a time. A session proceeds in rounds. In each round, the demonstrator controls one agent i i through a teleoperation interface for one or more episodes while every other agent j ≠ i j\neq i executes its current learned policy μ ψ j \mu_{\psi_{j}} . Every step of the episode is recorded as a joint transition, and the controlled agent’s pairs ( o i , a i ) (o_{i},a_{i}) form its cloning set 𝒟 i \mathcal{D}_{i} ; we also record the rewards observed at collection so that the transitions can later be replayed by RL. Control then passes to the next agent in round-robin order, and after each round every policy μ ψ j \mu_{\psi_{j}} is updated by behavior cloning, supervised regression from o j o_{j} to a j a_{j} , on 𝒟 j \mathcal{D}_{j} . Because the teammates run their current policies while a demonstration is given, the demonstrator reacts to the team as it actually behaves, which is what lets single-agent demonstrations produce cooperative behavior, and the data is collected on the state distribution the current team visits, which limits covariate shift. In the original work, 30–50 demonstrations per agent suffice for high task performance in simulation and on hardware. R2BC inherits the limits of behavior cloning: its performance is bounded by the demonstrator’s, deployment noise can still take the team to states no demonstration covered, and the last increments of performance cost the most demonstrations. IBMARL addresses these with online RL under a known team reward, using IBRL’s mechanism to decide, state by state, when the IL policy is still worth following. 4. Brown Affiliation: University of Utah , SLC, UT , USA email: daniel.s.brown@utah.edu 2027 Abstract. Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies 2.6 2.6 – 4.2 × 4.2\times faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline. Code, rollout videos and full results are available at https://zhanghutony.github.io/ibmarl/ . Keywords: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, Learning from Demonstration, Imitation Learning, Human-in-the-loop Learning 1. Introduction Cooperative multi-agent tasks are difficult for Reinforcement Learning (RL) to solve: the joint-action space grows exponentially with the number of agents, credit assignment across agents is ambiguous, and rewards are often inherently sparse ( Albrecht et al., 2024 ) . Even with a known model, finding an optimal joint policy for a finite-horizon Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) is NEXP-complete ( Bernstein et al., 2002 ) , so a learner that must also discover the reward through random joint exploration faces a search that grows with every agent added. In single-agent RL, demonstrations have been shown to help with this exploration problem, as examples of good behavior can often lead agents toward a reward signal even in sparse-reward tasks. Methods such as DQfD ( Hester et al., 2018 ) , DDPGfD ( Vecerik et al., 2017 ) , and DDPG + BC ( Nair et al., 2018 ) seed the replay buffer or regularize the learner toward expert data, and Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) ( Hu et al., 2024 ) goes further by keeping a behavior-cloned policy in the loop, using it to propose actions during exploration and to improve the bootstrap target (Sec. 3.1 ). Figure 1. IBMARL overview. (1) Teach: a human teleoperates one robot at a time while the others run their current IL policies (R2BC), producing a frozen IL policy for each robot. (2) Act: each robot’s IL and RL policies propose an action, and the centralized critic ensembles choose, per robot, which one the team executes. (3) Learn: the experience trains the critics, and each RL policy is pulled toward its IL action only where the critics prefer it. At deployment, each robot runs its RL policy alone. We address two obstacles that block the extension of such frameworks to MARL: (i) Demonstrations. Nearly all multi-agent imitation learning (MAIL) assumes joint demonstrations, in which an expert must simultaneously command all N N agents—data a lone human operator cannot realistically provide for collaborating teams ( Mattson et al., 2026 ; Turco et al., 2024 ) . To address this, we leverage Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) ( Mattson et al., 2026 ) (Sec. 3.2 ), which has the demonstrator cycle through controlling each agent of the team, while the other agents execute their current learned policies, yielding decentralized cooperative policies from realistic single-human demonstrations. However, R2BC inherits the limitations of behavior cloning: covariate shift, a performance ceiling at the demonstrator, and a prohibitive demonstration burden for the last increments of task performance. (ii) Decentralized execution. IBRL’s deployed policy relies on the critic at every step to choose between the IL action and the RL action. For a team, a critic that judges joint actions must have access to every agent’s observation and action, so keeping it during deployment would require centralized execution or communication. To avoid this, the RL actors must be deployable on their own, but nothing in IBRL ensures that they are, and the RL policies lag behind the policy that was actually executed during training (Sec. 6.3 ). We address both obstacles with Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL) , which keeps the R2BC policy in the loop rather than only in the data (Fig. 1 ). Assuming access to a task reward, we ask: Can MARL be bootstrapped from policies trained from realistic single-agent demonstrations, and can the result be deployed without the critics? During training (Fig. 1 , Act), every agent receives one action from its imitation policy and one from its RL actor, and centralized critic ensembles choose, per agent, which to execute. The same choice is made inside the TD target, so the critics learn the value of the better of the two policies rather than of the RL actors alone. RL thus improves on the R2BC policy where it is wrong while still following it where it is right, so the demonstrator’s ceiling of (i) is not inherited. For (ii), the critics’ preference also sets, state by state, how strongly each policy is pulled toward its imitation action (Fig. 1 , Learn), so the actors converge to the policy the critics execute and can be deployed alone, without the critics or the imitation policy. The contributions of this work are: (i) We formulate IBMARL , a generalization of IBRL to cooperative Dec-POMDPs in which the imitation-learned (IL) policy is a set of N N decentralized R2BC policies and a centralized critic ensemble arbitrates among per-agent combinations of IL and RL proposals. (ii) We introduce a gated imitation penalty that pulls each RL policy toward the IL proposal in proportion to the critics’ preference for it, so that the actors alone match the centralized policy and execution is decentralized. (iii) We evaluate IBMARL on four cooperative tasks in VMAS ( Bettini et al., 2022 ) using synthetic demonstrators. Here, IBMARL surpasses the IL policies 2.6 2.6 – 4.2 × 4.2\times faster than demonstration-based baselines on Navigation and 2.8 × 2.8\times faster on the physically coupled Buzzwire task, is the only method to surpass the IL policies on Balance and Transport, and exceeds the performance of the demonstrator on Buzzwire and Balance. (iv) We evaluate IBMARL with a real human operator using R2BC’s round-robin interface on Buzzwire, where IBMARL surpasses the human-trained IL policy more than twice as fast as the best baseline, suggesting that the gains carry over from synthetic to real demonstrators. 2. Related Work Single-Agent RL with Demonstrations: A significant body of prior work combines expert demonstrations with single-agent RL. In the simplest instantiation, offline demonstrations pretrain the starting policy by behavior cloning ( Ankile et al., 2025 ; Ramrakhya et al., 2023 ; Rajeswaran et al., 2018 ) or, for off-policy methods, populate the replay buffer with the demonstrated transitions ( Hester et al., 2018 ; Nair et al., 2020 ) . Both remove much of the early random exploration and give the critic high-value transitions from the start, which stabilizes early training and raises early returns over RL alone ( Rajeswaran et al., 2018 ; Hester et al., 2018 ; Kang et al., 2018 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) . A second family treats the demonstrations as offline data and adds a surrogate loss that keeps the policy or critic close to the demonstrated actions: DQfD’s large-margin term on the Double DQN loss ( Hester et al., 2018 ; Van Hasselt et al., 2016 ) , which surpasses both imitation and RL alone in nearly all of 42 Atari games within a million steps, and similar extensions in DDPGfD ( Vecerik et al., 2017 ) , POfD ( Kang et al., 2018 ) , NAC ( Gao et al., 2018 ) , Hybrid RL ( Song et al., 2023 ) and TD3+BC ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ) . When the reward is sparse, the demonstrations provide the signal: Nair et al. ( Nair et al., 2018 ) add a behavior-cloning loss to the DDPG policy and, for suboptimal demonstrations, gate it with a Q-filter so that it applies only where the critic rates the demonstrated action above the actor’s. IBRL ( Hu et al., 2024 ) keeps the imitation policy itself in the loop, letting the critic choose between its proposal and the actor’s at every step (Sec. 3.1 ). We propose IBMARL, the multi-agent generalization of IBRL; its gated imitation penalty is a soft, state-wise Q-filter applied to the IL policy’s action on the states the learner visits rather than to stored demonstrations. Multi-Agent RL with Demonstrations: Compared to the single-agent literature, MARL extensions that utilize demonstrations are few. Alagha et al. ( Alagha et al., 2023 ) let a synthetic expert take control of one agent during interaction so that part of the replay buffer is expert-provided, which improves early team performance; PRIMAL ( Sartoretti et al., 2019 ) trains decentralized policies by combining RL with imitation of a centralized planner; others reformulate particular MARL algorithms around demonstrations, namely MADDPG from demonstrations ( Qiu et al., 2023 ) , skill learning from demonstrations ( Venkatesh and Min, 2024 ) and hybrid training ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) ; a separate line imitates opponents in competitive games ( Bui et al., 2024 ) . The “-fD” regularizers above could in principle be added to QMIX ( Rashid et al., 2018 ) , VDN ( Sunehag et al., 2018 ) , FACMAC ( Peng et al., 2021 ) or LIIR ( Du et al., 2019 ) , but to our knowledge MADDPG from demonstrations ( Qiu et al., 2023 ) is the only work that has done so. By far the most relevant prior work is PegMARL ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , which also avoids joint demonstrations: single-agent demonstrations, given with no other agents present , train a behavioral discriminator and a transition discriminator that shape the sparse team reward online, leaving all teaching of cooperation to the reward. IBMARL differs in three ways. Its demonstrations are given through R2BC in the presence of teammates, so the IL policy already encodes cooperation; the IL policy acts through action proposals, bootstrap targets and a critic-gated pull on the policy rather than through reward shaping or a scheduled cloning penalty ( Nair et al., 2018 ; Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ) ; and the output is a set of decentralized actors that need neither the centralized critics nor the IL policy at run time. 3. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.18533 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Nov 2026] Title: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL Authors: Zelin He , Siyu Zhu , Jacob Helwig , Yujian Liu , Li An , Rohit Jain , Shiyu Chang , Alborz Geramifard View a PDF of the paper titled ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL, by Zelin He and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model's behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task's data and evolved with the model.
