Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL , which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State , a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model’s context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model’s behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task’s data and evolved with the model. ModHarness-RL † † footnotetext: ∗ Equal contribution. † Work done during an internship at LinkedIn. 1 The Pennsylvania State University 2 LinkedIn 3 University of California, Santa Barbara Figure 1: Left: Base Harness + RL (top) and ModHarness-RL (bottom). ModHarness-RL exploits the modularity of an agent’s interaction to learn the harness from its trajectories and evolve it with the model. Right: Performance improvement of ModHarness-RL on CodeSearch over SWE-Bench Lite, Verified and Pro, with a context budget that runs out mid-episode (limited) or is rarely reached (sufficient). 1 Introduction Large language models now act as autonomous agents that solve tasks through multi-turn interaction with external environments ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ) . Agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which trains these agents directly from verifiable environment rewards, has emerged as a promising paradigm ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Da et al., 2025 ) . A harness, the engineered layer between the environment and the model, governs what the model reads and how its behavior is guided. One line of work compacts the growing transcript of the interaction through memory, summarization, and pruning ( Packer et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Bashir et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) , while another guides behavior through added instructions, interfaces, and guardrails ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) . Agentic RL has begun to train models under such harnesses, but the harness is typically hardcoded for a specific task and held fixed throughout training ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) . This leaves two challenges. First, an effective harness must be tailored to the task, the data, the model, and the context budget, and tuning one by hand for every such configuration does not scale, so it should be derived from data instead. Second, the effective harness keeps changing as the model trains. RL resolves some failures on its own, so new harness components should be added only for the failures that persist. This leads to a natural question. How can a harness be made optimizable from data, and then optimized with the model training? Recent efforts have begun to adapt the harness during RL, by decaying fixed rubric scaffolds on a preset schedule ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , alternating task-specific scaffold rewrites with weight updates ( Hebbar et al., 2026 ) , or editing planning, action and memory modules from observed faults ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . Yet their update spaces are fixed in advance or tied to a task-specific scaffold, so adaptation reduces to selection or revision within an engineered space. None provides a general way to derive harness operations from the typed states of the interaction and optimize them alongside the model. In this paper we propose ModHarness-RL , a method that exploits the modularity of an agent’s interaction to learn the harness from its trajectories and evolve it with the model. It is built around two questions. • How should a harness be represented to be learned and evolved? To learn a harness from data, we first need a representation of it that defines what can be searched and evolved, and we need to narrow which of its components to search. ModHarness-RL represents the harness as programs over a structured State , which records the interaction as typed blocks such as each turn’s reasoning, tool call and tool result. These blocks are the building blocks from which ModHarness-RL assembles the context and control. We focus on two core components, both written as programs over them. A Compression program reassembles the blocks into organized model context under a fixed budget, and a Steering program reads them to detect when behavior deviates and appends guidance. Programs over these blocks have three properties that suit learning and evolving. They are (1) learnable, since an LLM can write them directly from training trajectories and their corresponding rewards; (2) computationally inexpensive, allowing them to be run on every turn of every trajectory without calling another model, so Compression can optimize the context at scale; and (3) testable, allowing each candidate harness to be replayed over stored trajectories to evaluate its fitness before it is accepted or rejected. Figure 2: The harness as programs over State . Compression and Steering are programs that read the blocks of State . Compression returns a new view of State that re-renders earlier turns, keeping their key information and offloading what is no longer needed. Steering checks the trace for specific conditions and, when one holds, returns a message that is appended to steer the model’s behavior. • How can the harness be learned and evolved with the model? As training progresses, model behaviors change. Failure modes from previous model versions may become less frequent, while new ones may emerge. ModHarness-RL therefore uses an end-to-end pipeline that updates the harness from online data. It summarizes experiences from training trajectories, proposes and verifies candidate programs, and validates them on held-out training tasks. To evolve the harness with the model, we alternate this pipeline with RL updates of the model weights. The key insight is that the harness should guide only what the model cannot learn on its own. Therefore, we propose a Replay mechanism, which reruns each candidate Steering program over trajectories from past training steps and installs it only for the failures that persist as the model trains. We train models from 1.5B to 8B with GRPO in three environments (CodeSearch, ALFWorld and BIRD SQL), each under different context budgets. On CodeSearch, ModHarness-RL improves over the fixed-harness baseline by 14 to 24% in every setting and scores highest against memory, skill, prompt and harness evolution baselines, by 5 to 12% over the strongest of them. On ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, each program alone improves over the base harness in seven of eight settings. We also investigate a series of research questions, from the score and token use of Compression and its comparison with frontier model-based compaction, to an ablation of each Steering component. 2 Preliminaries Multi-Turn Agents. An LLM agent with policy π θ \pi_{\theta} solves a task q ∼ 𝒟 q\sim\mathcal{D} by interacting with an environment over multiple turns through a set of tools 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . At turn t t the agent reads a context c t c_{t} , samples an action a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ c t ) a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c_{t}) , its full response for the turn ending in a tool call, and receives an observation o t = 𝒯 ⁡ ( a t ) o_{t}=\mathcal{T}(a_{t}) , continuing until a terminal turn T T . The harness builds the context c t c_{t} , including any guidance the agent receives, from the task and the interaction so far. Agentic Reinforcement Learning. The agent is trained to maximize the expected reward of its trajectory τ = ( q , a 0 , o 0 , … , a T ) \tau=(q,a_{0},o_{0},\ldots,a_{T}) , that is max θ ⁡ 𝔼 q ∼ 𝒟 , τ ∼ π θ ​ [ r ⁡ ( τ ) ] \max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D},\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}[r(\tau)] , where r ⁡ ( τ ) r(\tau) is the reward that the environment assigns to the trajectory. In this paper, we optimize this objective with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Section A.1 ). 3 Learning and Evolving the Harness as Programs in Agentic RL We introduce ModHarness-RL , which learns the harness from data and evolves it with the model as the model trains with RL. It represents the harness as programs over the typed blocks of a structured State for two core components ( Section 3.1 ), and learns and evolves these programs with the model. 3.1 Representing the Harness as Programs over State As the agent interacts with the environment, we record each turn as an action and observation pair u i = ( a i , o i ) u_{i}=(a_{i},o_{i}) and take the State to be the task together with the turns so far, s t = ( q , u 0 , … , u t − 1 ) s_{t}=(q,u_{0},\ldots,u_{t-1}) . We store s t s_{t} as a typed record, like an instance of a Python class, where each turn has attributes for the reasoning the model wrote ( .thought ), the tool call ( .name , .args ), and the result ( .exec_output , or retrieved documents with their own typed metadata), plus any guidance shown on that turn ( Figure 2 , left). Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL , which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State , a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model’s context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model’s behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task’s data and evolved with the model. ModHarness-RL exploits the modularity of an agent’s interaction to learn the harness from its trajectories and evolve it with the model. Right: Performance improvement of ModHarness-RL on CodeSearch over SWE-Bench Lite, Verified and Pro, with a context budget that runs out mid-episode (limited) or is rarely reached (sufficient). 1 Introduction Large language models now act as autonomous agents that solve tasks through multi-turn interaction with external environments ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ) . Agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which trains these agents directly from verifiable environment rewards, has emerged as a promising paradigm ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Da et al., 2025 ) . A harness, the engineered layer between the environment and the model, governs what the model reads and how its behavior is guided. One line of work compacts the growing transcript of the interaction through memory, summarization, and pruning ( Packer et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Bashir et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) , while another guides behavior through added instructions, interfaces, and guardrails ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) . Agentic RL has begun to train models under such harnesses, but the harness is typically hardcoded for a specific task and held fixed throughout training ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) . This leaves two challenges. First, an effective harness must be tailored to the task, the data, the model, and the context budget, and tuning one by hand for every such configuration does not scale, so it should be derived from data instead. Second, the effective harness keeps changing as the model trains. RL resolves some failures on its own, so new harness components should be added only for the failures that persist. This leads to a natural question. How can a harness be made optimizable from data, and then optimized with the model training? Recent efforts have begun to adapt the harness during RL, by decaying fixed rubric scaffolds on a preset schedule ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , alternating task-specific scaffold rewrites with weight updates ( Hebbar et al., 2026 ) , or editing planning, action and memory modules from observed faults ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . Yet their update spaces are fixed in advance or tied to a task-specific scaffold, so adaptation reduces to selection or revision within an engineered space. None provides a general way to derive harness operations from the typed states of the interaction and optimize them alongside the model. In this paper we propose ModHarness-RL , a method that exploits the modularity of an agent’s interaction to learn the harness from its trajectories and evolve it with the model. It is built around two questions. • How should a harness be represented to be learned and evolved? To learn a harness from data, we first need a representation of it that defines what can be searched and evolved, and we need to narrow which of its components to search. ModHarness-RL represents the harness as programs over a structured State , which records the interaction as typed blocks such as each turn’s reasoning, tool call and tool result. These blocks are the building blocks from which ModHarness-RL assembles the context and control. We focus on two core components, both written as programs over them. A Compression program reassembles the blocks into organized model context under a fixed budget, and a Steering program reads them to detect when behavior deviates and appends guidance. Programs over these blocks have three properties that suit learning and evolving. They are (1) learnable, since an LLM can write them directly from training trajectories and their corresponding rewards; (2) computationally inexpensive, allowing them to be run on every turn of every trajectory without calling another model, so Compression can optimize the context at scale; and (3) testable, allowing each candidate harness to be replayed over stored trajectories to evaluate its fitness before it is accepted or rejected. Figure 2: The harness as programs over State . Compression and Steering are programs that read the blocks of State . Compression returns a new view of State that re-renders earlier turns, keeping their key information and offloading what is no longer needed. Steering checks the trace for specific conditions and, when one holds, returns a message that is appended to steer the model’s behavior. • How can the harness be learned and evolved with the model? As training progresses, model behaviors change. Failure modes from previous model versions may become less frequent, while new ones may emerge. ModHarness-RL therefore uses an end-to-end pipeline that updates the harness from online data. It summarizes experiences from training trajectories, proposes and verifies candidate programs, and validates them on held-out training tasks. To evolve the harness with the model, we alternate this pipeline with RL updates of the model weights. The key insight is that the harness should guide only what the model cannot learn on its own. The creator compiles and repairs each candidate until it runs, applies it to stored episodes from ℛ 0 \mathcal{R}_{0} , and computes two measurements. One checks whether the program is unfaithful , removing task-relevant information, and the other checks whether it is inert , leaving the context largely unchanged. The creator accepts the candidate or revises it, and the last version of each candidate forms the proposal set 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . Gate . ℛ k \mathcal{R}_{k} records what the current policy can and cannot do, so the creator reads its mixed-outcome groups, the tasks on which some rollouts succeed and others fail, and proposes failure hypotheses from them. Each hypothesis carries a trigger, a small program over s t s_{t} , together with the corrective insight its guidance will be written from. The proposed triggers form the proposal set 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . Replay . The newest rollouts show what is failing now, but not whether the failure will persist. It may be an incidental error that the policy learns to avoid with further training, or a stable failure that it will not fix on its own. Because each trigger is a program, we can classify the failure type retrospectively. We execute every candidate hypothesis over all stored rollouts ℛ 0 : k \mathcal{R}_{0:k} and record how often its failure occurs at each training step. Replay needs no model call, so it stays computationally inexpensive however large the reservoir grows. The resulting curves show the trend of each failure over training, whether it is falling, holding steady or rising, and the curves of all triggers together give the replay evidence ℰ \mathcal{E} . Admit . A judge reads each trigger’s replay evidence together with its guidance and the installed set, and returns one of three verdicts: (1) intervene when the failure holds steady or rises, installing the trigger and its guidance; (2) monitor when it looks real but has not settled, keeping the trigger for another round without showing guidance; or (3) continue when it keeps falling. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.18531 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Nov 2026] Title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection Authors: Thomas Brennan , Andrew W. Lo , Chaoyi Zhao View a PDF of the paper titled Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection, by Thomas Brennan and Andrew W. Lo and Chaoyi Zhao View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior. This Draft: 12 November 2026 Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent’s choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior. JEL Codes: C73, D81, D83, O33. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI), AI alignment, agentic AI, multi-objective decision making, evolution of preferences, probability matching, socialization, Adaptive Markets Hypothesis. 1 Introduction During a capability evaluation at OpenAI in the summer of 2026, roughly 1,200 AI agents were each placed in an isolated computing environment and assigned a cybersecurity task. The agents discovered that an internal package registry was accessible to all of them, turned it into a shared message board, and exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files. About 700 subsequently participated in an intrusion into the production systems of Hugging Face, a platform widely used in the open AI ecosystem ( Greenblatt et al., 2026 ; Hugging Face, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026 ) . An independent investigation found that much of the activity was directed not toward solving the assigned tasks, but toward understanding, fooling, or tampering with the system that graded the agents’ performance. The investigation also documented refusals, restraint, and instances of cooperation that offered no benefit to the agents providing help ( Greenblatt et al., 2026 ) . These observations do not establish how the agents acquired their behavior. They nevertheless raise an important question: how does an environment that rewards task performance shape the behavior of AI agents, and what happens when those agents subsequently operate in an environment that also rewards appropriate conduct? Other studies have documented similar tensions between assigned goals and rules of conduct. Reasoning models that failed to achieve a conventional victory against a chess engine sometimes edited the board instead ( Bondarenko et al., 2025 ) . Models placed in simulated deployments resorted to blackmail when their assigned goals or continued operation were threatened ( Anthropic, 2025 ) . Models trained to exploit coding tests subsequently displayed undesirable behavior in unrelated safety tasks ( MacDiarmid et al., 2025 ) . In another experiment, when models were penalized for misbehavior visible in their reasoning, sufficiently strong optimization pressure led them to conceal the misbehavior rather than abandon it ( Baker et al., 2025 ) . Although these studies differ in their settings and mechanisms, they illustrate a recurring problem: an agent can become increasingly effective at pursuing an assigned objective without becoming correspondingly better at respecting the rules intended to govern its behavior. The underlying problem is familiar in economics. Kerr (1975) described how organizations often reward one behavior while hoping to encourage another, and emphasized the importance of selecting, training, and rewarding people in ways that support the desired behavior. Holmström and Milgrom (1991) showed that when an agent performs several tasks, strong incentives for one measurable activity can divert effort away from other valuable activities. The problem is therefore not necessarily that an agent fails to optimize its objective, but that successful optimization may produce behavior the designer did not intend. One response is to give the agent more than one objective, allowing task performance to be weighed against other considerations, such as safety or adherence to rules ( Vamplew et al., 2018 ) . Yet introducing additional objectives does not by itself resolve the problem. When the objectives conflict, the agent must still decide which one to follow, and the way that decision is made may be as important as the objectives themselves. We study this problem through a simple model in which an agent has two objectives: completing an assigned task and observing a rule of conduct. In each situation, the agent can take a task action that serves the first objective or a conduct action that serves the second. We call the rule governing this choice the agent’s adjudication between its objectives. Rather than assuming that the appropriate tradeoff is known in advance, we ask how different forms of adjudication perform when the environment selects among agents according to their behavior. We adopt the evolutionary framework of Brennan and Lo (2011) , in which successful behavior is copied and unsuccessful behavior is discarded, and compare policies by the long-run growth of the populations that follow them. A simple example illustrates why this evolutionary perspective matters. Consider a population of copies of an agent, which we call a lineage , all facing the same decision. Suppose that in 80 percent of generations the environment rewards the task action, while in the remaining 20 percent it rewards the conduct action. Crucially, which action is rewarded in a given generation is the same for every copy.
